prompt: What separates structured, semi-structured and unstructured data, according to this lesson?
hint: It is a question with one word in it: where.

choices.text: The file extension the data is saved with
choices.why: The extension says how bytes are laid out, not whether anybody checked them.

choices.text: How much of the data there is in total
choices.why: A huge table is still structured, and one email is still unstructured.

choices.text: Where the schema lives
choices.why: Right: in the table, in each record, or nowhere.

choices.text: Whether a person or a machine produced it
choices.why: Machines write free text too, and people fill in tables.

prompt: A CSV file has a header line naming its columns. Why is that not enough to make its data structured in this lesson’s sense?
hint: Look at what the header leaves out.

choices.text: It names columns but declares no types
choices.why: Right: `12` and `12 min` sit in one column without complaint.

choices.text: The header is optional, so most CSV files leave it out
choices.why: Whether it is there or not, it carries names only.

choices.text: CSV cannot hold more than one table per file
choices.why: True, and irrelevant: one table can still be unchecked.

choices.text: Commas inside values break the columns apart
choices.why: Quoting handles that; lesson 6 shows it. The missing piece is types.

prompt: Roda Livre’s app events arrive as JSON, and a program checks each one against a strict description before storing it, refusing any that differ. Which shape does that data behave like?
hint: The format is one thing; the check is another.

choices.text: Semi-structured, because the file is JSON
choices.why: That sorts by format. A check at the door is what makes data structured.

choices.text: Unstructured, since nothing in it is a table yet
choices.why: Every field has a name; nothing has to be interpreted.

choices.text: A fourth shape the lesson does not name
choices.why: The three cover it: the question is where the schema lives.

choices.text: Structured, since it is checked on the way in
choices.why: Right: declared first, checked on write, like a table.

prompt: Which of these is unstructured data at Roda Livre?
hint: Where is the meaning kept?

choices.text: The station list in the app’s database
choices.why: A table with declared columns: structured.

choices.text: A recording of a customer’s call to the help line about a dock
choices.why: Right: the meaning is in the sound, and somebody has to interpret it.

choices.text: The JSON event sent when a ride ends
choices.why: Names travel with the values: semi-structured.

choices.text: A sensor message with a dock id and a time
choices.why: Named fields: semi-structured at worst.

prompt: Match each shape to where its schema lives.
hint: One of them has no schema at all.

pairs.right: in the table, declared before the data
in each record, beside the values
nowhere; the meaning is in the content

prompt: In `structured.py`, what happened to the ride whose `minutes` was `"9 min"`?
hint: Read the last line the program printed.

choices.text: It was stored with an empty value for `minutes`
choices.why: pyarrow did not fill anything in; it refused.

choices.text: It was stored as the number 9, with the text dropped
choices.why: Nothing guessed at the number; the value was refused whole.

choices.text: It was refused, and the call built no table at all
choices.why: Right: the call raised an error and built nothing.

choices.text: It was stored, and the error appeared when reading
choices.why: That is what `loose.py` did. Here the check ran on write.

prompt: `loose.py` and `structured.py` met the same `"9 min"`. What was different about the failure in `loose.py`?
hint: Who was running the program when it stopped?

choices.text: It surfaced at the reader, after the file was stored
choices.why: Right: the writer was never told.

choices.text: It printed a wrong total and carried on
choices.why: It stopped with a `ValueError`; it was loud, just late.

choices.text: It never failed, because CSV has a text type for every value
choices.why: The write succeeded, but the sum on line 17 failed.

choices.text: It failed earlier, as soon as the file was opened
choices.why: Opening and reading worked; adding up the minutes did not.

prompt: Checking every value against a declared schema at the moment it is stored is called schema on ___.
hint: The opposite of reading.

prompt: Why is `started_at` declared as a timestamp in `structured.py` rather than as a string?
hint: Think about every reader after the writer.

choices.text: A string column would make the table larger on disk
choices.why: Size is not the reason given; meaning is.

choices.text: pyarrow cannot store dates written as text
choices.why: It can store any text; then it would be a string, not a time.

choices.text: Strings cannot carry the São Paulo time zone
choices.why: The JSON events carry `-03:00` inside a string. What they lack is a type.

choices.text: So every reader gets a time, not text to parse
choices.why: Right: sorting and grouping by hour work directly.

prompt: Marta asks for a new column, `helmet`, in the rides table. In a structured table, what does that take?
hint: What did the section call changing a schema later?

choices.text: Nothing: the next rows can include it
choices.why: That is semi-structured data. A table refuses a field it does not have.

choices.text: A deliberate change to the schema
choices.why: Right: a migration, made on purpose and agreed with the readers.

choices.text: A new table, because tables can never change
choices.why: Tables change; the change is just deliberate.

choices.text: Converting the whole table to JSON first
choices.why: Changing the format would throw away the check that made the table worth having.

prompt: How many of the six events of 15 September have an `end`?
hint: The `grep -c` count.

prompt: Ride `R000104` has no `end` in its event. What does that mean?
hint: Look at what the generator does every fourth ride.

choices.text: The event was cut short in transit
choices.why: The line is complete JSON; nothing was lost.

choices.text: The app has a bug that drops the field at random
choices.why: It is absent on purpose, every fourth ride.

choices.text: The bicycle was returned to its own start station
choices.why: Those rides do have an `end`: R000103 and R000105.

choices.text: It had not ended when the event was sent
choices.why: Right, and a reader that fills in a default would report it finished.

prompt: Which of these are types a JSON value can have? Choose all that apply.
hint: Six types, and one notable absence.

choices.text: array
choices.why: Yes: `charges` is one.

choices.text: timestamp
choices.why: No: `at` is a string that looks like a time.

choices.text: object
choices.why: Yes: `bike` is one.

choices.text: null
choices.why: Yes, one of the six.

prompt: Why does `charges` not fit in a single table column?
hint: Count the charges of two different rides.

choices.text: It is a list, and its length varies from one ride to the next
choices.why: Right: a cell holds one value, and a ride has one to three charges.

choices.text: Its items are objects, and tables only hold numbers
choices.why: Tables hold text and times too. The trouble is how many there are.

choices.text: Its values are in cents rather than in reais
choices.why: The unit has nothing to do with the shape.

choices.text: It is nested two levels deeper than `bike` is
choices.why: `bike` is nested too, and flattens fine. Arrays are the problem.

prompt: With schema on read, who decides what a missing `coupon` means?
hint: Nothing was declared at the door.

choices.text: The JSON standard, which defines missing as null
choices.why: JSON says nothing about a key that is not there.

choices.text: The app team, who sent the event
choices.why: They decided to leave it out; what it means downstream is not theirs to enforce.

choices.text: Each program that reads the events
choices.why: Right, which is why two readers can decide differently.

choices.text: The file, through its first line
choices.why: JSON Lines has no header; each line stands alone.

prompt: How many rows did exploding `charges` produce for the six rides of 15 September?
hint: The line ending in `charge rows`.

prompt: After the explode, somebody counts rows in the charges table to report how many rides there were. What do they get?
hint: One row there is not one ride.

choices.text: Six, because every row carries a `ride_id`
choices.why: Carrying the id does not make the rows distinct; counting distinct ids would.

choices.text: An error, because the table has no ride column
choices.why: It has `ride_id`, and nothing stops a count.

choices.text: Five, because the ride in progress has no charges
choices.why: R000104 has its unlock charge.

choices.text: Twelve: one row per charge, which is not one row per ride
choices.why: Right: a quiet overcount, as trustworthy-looking as the right answer.

prompt: What does flattening do to the nested object `bike`?
hint: The program joins names with a dot.

choices.text: Moves it into a table of its own, one row per bicycle
choices.why: That is the explode, which the lesson keeps for arrays.

choices.text: Drops it, since only top-level fields become columns
choices.why: `flat` walks into it; only lists are skipped.

choices.text: Stores the whole object as one text column
choices.why: Possible, but then every reader parses JSON again. The program does not.

choices.text: Makes columns `bike.id` and `bike.battery`
choices.why: Right: still one row per event, with longer names.

prompt: How many columns did `flatten.py` discover in the events of 15 September?
hint: The first line of its output.

prompt: The sum of cents across the exploded charges table, 3425, is correct. Summing `end.minutes` across the same table is not. Why the difference?
hint: Ask what each number belongs to.

choices.text: Cents are whole numbers and minutes are not whole
choices.why: Both are integers in the events. The difference is which table they belong to.

choices.text: Minutes belong to the ride, and a ride repeats
choices.why: Right: each charge is there once; each ride is there two or three times.

choices.text: The ride in progress has no minutes, which spoils the total
choices.why: A missing value would make the sum smaller, not repeated.

choices.text: The explode sorted the rows, and minutes depend on order
choices.why: A sum does not depend on order.

prompt: What did version 4.2 of the app change in the events of 16 September?
hint: The last two lines `drift.py` printed.

choices.text: It removed `coupon` and renamed `end` to `finish`
choices.why: Nothing was reported gone; both are still there.

choices.text: It started sending every event twice over
choices.why: That is a duplicate, not a change of shape.

choices.text: Battery became text; `helmet` was added
choices.why: Right: one type change and one new field.

choices.text: It moved `station` out of `start` to the top level
choices.why: The paths are unchanged; `drift.py` would have reported both.

prompt: Why is the changed type of `bike.battery` more dangerous than the new field `helmet`?
hint: Which one does an existing reader touch?

choices.text: Readers that already exist sum and average the battery
choices.why: Right: something already sums it, and now meets `"58%"`.

choices.text: New fields are refused by JSON, so `helmet` is dropped
choices.why: JSON refuses nothing; `helmet` arrived fine.

choices.text: A boolean takes less space than a percentage string
choices.why: Size is not the danger; what readers do with the value is.

choices.text: `helmet` is in a different file from the battery
choices.why: Both are in every event of 16 September.

prompt: The battery values `"100%"` and `"58%"` are loaded into a text column. What happens when a chart sorts by battery?
hint: Text is compared one character at a time.

choices.text: The load fails, because text cannot be sorted
choices.why: Text sorts; it sorts by characters, not by value.

choices.text: The database removes the `%` and sorts the numbers
choices.why: Nothing strips it; the column holds text.

choices.text: `"100%"` sorts before `"58%"`, and the chart is wrong without any error
choices.why: Right: `1` sorts before `5`, and nothing complains.

choices.text: A `TypeError` stops the chart from drawing
choices.why: That is Python adding numbers to text. Sorting text raises nothing.

prompt: The shape of incoming data changing without anybody downstream being told is called schema ___.
hint: A boat without an anchor does it.

prompt: Order these places to notice drift, from the cheapest to the most expensive.
hint: The later it is noticed, the more data holds both shapes.
items: a check on each batch, at the door
a report that breaks in a reader
trap: Never noticing is the most expensive, because every number built on it is wrong.

prompt: In a support email, which part is unstructured?
hint: Which part has no field names?

choices.text: The list of attachments and their sizes
choices.why: Named fields: metadata, structured.

choices.text: The time it was received
choices.why: A field with a name and a type.

choices.text: The id of the customer who sent it
choices.why: Metadata again: `C0042` is a value in a named field.

choices.text: The body the customer wrote
choices.why: Right: the meaning is in the words.

prompt: Of the six emails, how many did the pattern in `emails.py` match to the right station?
hint: Read the last column against the bodies.

prompt: Why did email M05 produce `ST10` when it is not about a station?
hint: The customer lives somewhere.

choices.text: Batel is also the neighbourhood the customer lives in, and the pattern cannot tell
choices.why: Right: the pattern matches the word, not the meaning.

choices.text: The customer’s id happens to contain the code ST10
choices.why: The pattern searches the body only, and C0019 is not ST10.

choices.text: Regular expressions guess when nothing matches exactly
choices.why: A pattern never guesses; it found the exact word.

choices.text: The app attached the customer’s location to the body
choices.why: The body is what the customer wrote, word for word.

prompt: Which emails named a station that the pattern missed? Choose all that apply.
hint: Look for a `-` in the last column.

choices.text: M03, “the Botanical Garden”
choices.why: Yes: the name in English.
Yes: XV written as a number.

choices.text: M02, Largo da Ordem
choices.why: No: found, as ST06.

choices.text: M06, “Opera de Arame”
choices.why: Yes: the accent was missing.

prompt: A language model starts extracting stations from the emails. Which habit from the section matters most once it does?
hint: Its output is a derived value.

choices.text: Deleting the email bodies once the station has been extracted
choices.why: The originals are what a better extractor runs on next year.

choices.text: Trusting its answers, since it reads like a person does
choices.why: It is wrong some of the time too, in its own ways.

choices.text: Recording which program made each value
choices.why: Right, with the original kept beside it.

choices.text: Mixing its values into the column staff type by hand
choices.why: Then nobody can tell a guess from a fact.

prompt: Marta asks how many complaints arrived on Monday and from how many customers. What does answering it need?
hint: Which part of an email holds the date and the sender?

choices.text: A model that reads every body
choices.why: Nothing in the question is inside the body.

choices.text: The station pattern from `emails.py`, extended
choices.why: Stations are not part of the question.

choices.text: The photos attached to each complaint
choices.why: Counting them needs metadata, not pixels.

choices.text: Only the metadata of each email
choices.why: Right: time and customer are named fields.

prompt: Match each statement to the approach it describes.
hint: Ask when the check runs.

pairs.left: the writer hears about a bad value
each reader repeats the same check

prompt: Caio strips the `%` from `bike.battery`, and an analyst skips the rows that have one. What follows?
hint: One file, two readers, two decisions.

choices.text: Both get the same average, since the data in the file is the same
choices.why: The data is the same; their checks are not.

choices.text: Two different averages from one file, each of them confident
choices.why: Right: the same check, written twice, disagreeing.

choices.text: The file refuses the second reader
choices.why: A stored file refuses no reader; only a write can be refused.

choices.text: An error in both programs, because JSON forbids `%`
choices.why: `"58%"` is a valid JSON string.

prompt: A batch is refused by a strict check at three in the morning. What is the cost that schema on write adds here and schema on read does not?
hint: What was stored?

choices.text: Every reader must check the batch again later
choices.why: That is schema on read’s cost, not this one.

choices.text: The bad values are stored and spread to readers
choices.why: The refusal is exactly what stopped them being stored.

choices.text: The refused batch is stored nowhere, and somebody has to fetch it again
choices.why: Right: somebody has to fetch it again.

choices.text: The table loses the schema it had declared
choices.why: The schema is untouched; the batch is what is gone.

prompt: Put the steps of Roda Livre’s app events in the order a platform runs them.
hint: Land first, decide later.
items: the app sends a JSON event
the event lands as it came in the raw zone
a nightly job flattens and checks it
trap: The raw zone comes before the check, so nothing is lost to a check that was too strict.

prompt: Match each kind of storage to what it is built around.
hint: Tables, documents, bytes.

prompt: Where do the photos customers attach of a damaged bicycle most naturally go?
hint: The store does not need to look inside them.

choices.text: A column of the rides table, with one photo per ride
choices.why: A photo belongs to a complaint, and pixels in a table cell help no query.

choices.text: A document store, so the pixels can be queried by field
choices.why: Pixels have no fields to query.

choices.text: Nowhere: unstructured data is not worth keeping
choices.why: The originals are what a better extractor will run on.

choices.text: Object storage, metadata beside it
choices.why: Right: the bytes as they came, and rows that say what they are.

prompt: What does a document store let you do that this lesson’s `flatten.py` had to do by hand first?
hint: Think of `bike.battery` below 20.

choices.text: Find documents by a field nested inside them, such as `bike.battery`
choices.why: Right: no flattening first.

choices.text: Refuse documents whose types differ from the first one
choices.why: It does not require documents to agree; that is the price.

choices.text: Store photos and recordings beside the events
choices.why: That is object storage’s job.

choices.text: Turn `"58%"` back into the number 58 when reading
choices.why: Every query still has to cope with it.

prompt: A table in SQLite has a column declared `INTEGER`, and the table is not `STRICT`. Somebody inserts `"9 min"`. What happens?
hint: The section named SQLite’s one difference.

choices.text: SQLite refuses the row, like any relational database
choices.why: Only a `STRICT` table refuses it.

choices.text: SQLite converts it to the number 9 and drops the text
choices.why: It keeps the value as it came.

choices.text: The value is stored, wrong type and all
choices.why: Right: the check a table usually gives is not there.

choices.text: The whole database file becomes unreadable
choices.why: Nothing is damaged; one value is simply the wrong type.

prompt: A sensor sends `{"dock": "ST03-07", "bike": null, "at": "2025-09-15T08:00:00-03:00"}` every minute, and the data team stores it as it arrives. Which shape is it?
hint: Names beside values, nothing checked first.

choices.text: Structured, because every message has the same three fields every minute
choices.why: Today they agree; nothing makes tomorrow’s agree.

choices.text: Unstructured, because a sensor is not a person
choices.why: Who wrote it does not matter; the fields have names.

choices.text: Semi-structured: named fields, stored with nothing checked at the door
choices.why: Right: JSON stored as it came, schema on read.

choices.text: None of the three, because `bike` is null
choices.why: null is a JSON value like any other.

prompt: `drift.py` reported nothing between two batches, but every event in the second has `minutes` in seconds rather than minutes. Why did it stay silent?
hint: What does it compare?

choices.text: It only compares field names and types
choices.why: Right: an int is still an int. Values need checks of their own, lesson 7’s.

choices.text: It reads only the first line of each file
choices.why: It reads every line; `infer` loops over the file.

choices.text: Seconds and minutes are both stored as strings in JSON
choices.why: They are numbers; the type did not change.

choices.text: It ignores fields nested inside `end`
choices.why: It walks into nested objects; `end.minutes` is in its report.

prompt: What was the sum of all the charges of 15 September, in cents?
hint: The last line of `flatten.py`.

prompt: Turning an array into a second table, one row per item, each carrying the id of its parent, is called an ___.
hint: Spark’s name for it.

prompt: A new partner sends Roda Livre a nightly CSV whose columns change whenever their staff edit the spreadsheet. Which arrangement does this lesson argue for?
hint: Land first; decide in one place.

choices.text: Refuse every file that differs, and keep only the ones that fit
choices.why: Then a changed file is stored nowhere and has to be fetched again.

choices.text: Keep the raw file, check it in one job
choices.why: Right: nothing lost, and one check feeding the curated tables.

choices.text: Let each analyst read the CSV and adapt as it changes
choices.why: The same check written by every reader, and they will disagree.

choices.text: Convert it to JSON, since JSON copes with any shape
choices.why: A new format moves the problem; nobody has checked anything yet.
